PR Summary by Qodo

Stop promise interval ticks when aborted during queue draining 🐞 Bug fix 🧪 Tests 🕐 10-20 Minutes
AI Description

>
>• Clear promise interval timers immediately on abort so slow consumers cannot accumulate new ticks.
>• Preserve already queued ticks, then reject the iterator with ABORT_ERR and the signal’s reason.
>• Regenerate the guest module and add a fake-timer regression for the source shim.
>
Merge Risk 🟡 Medium

Blast radius 🟢 Low 💥 1 capability

- 1 affected end-to-end capability after fault-specific containment; implementation boundaries do not widen its functional scope. - The source shim is the producer implementation for the timers/promises builtin, the prepare script maps that builtin to the shim, and the generated guest artifact is the shipped representation. - These are propagation hops of one end-to-end timer compatibility behavior, not independent capabilities. - The inspected runtime conformance consumer uses the same timers/promises compatibility surface.
Behavioral complexity 🔴 High 🧩 Interacting branches, Concurrent ordering

- Before: abort only woke the pending iterator; the native interval remained scheduled until iterator finalization, while queued ticks and abort state were coordinated by the loop. - After: abort additionally clears the native interval immediately, wakes the waiter, and the loop must still drain ticks already counted before observing the aborted signal and rejecting. - The new correctness condition is that cancellation must stop future producer ticks without losing already queued ticks or changing the required abort rejection ordering. - This is a small state/ordering interaction between the interval callback, abort event, pending waiter, queued tick count, and async-generator finally block; it does not introduce a new algorithm or persistent invariant.
Potential damage 🟡 Medium 🩹 Recoverable

- If this capability regresses, an aborted interval may fail to stop promptly, fail to deliver queued ticks in the expected order, or fail to reject the iterator as expected. - The consequence is limited to the timer consumer's control flow and possible temporary timer/resource retention; there is no changed persistent state, cross-tenant data, or external side effect in this path. - Reverting the code restores future behavior. - An already-created leaking iterator would require iterator.return\(\), task termination, or process teardown; no automatic repair worker or persistent-state repair path is established. - Revert restores the implementation for new invocations. - Active iterators can be explicitly closed with return\(\) or cleaned up when their guest invocation terminates; no durable state repair or external compensation is required.
Assessed commit 14bcd63
Diagram

```mermaid graph TD T["Interval timer"] --> Q["Queued ticks"] --> I["Async iterator"] --> D{"Queue drained?"} S["Abort signal"] --> L["Abort listener"] -->|clear| T L -->|wake| I D -->|pending ticks| I D -->|aborted| E["ABORT_ERR"] ```
High-Level Assessment

>Clearing the timer in the abort listener is the direct fix: it stops production even while the iterator is suspended at a yield, without discarding queued ticks. Checking the signal only in the iterator or timer callback would leave the timer scheduled during that interval.
